A frequency effect, 14 bytes for command $D4 (the title, voices 1 and 3): a slide of +0 for 10 frames, then -100 for 10 frames after 1 frame, then again from the start.

Frequency effect steps, 10 bytes for command $D2 (the title, voices 2 and 3): $00 $09 $05 $0C $01 $85 $00 $09, read as four 16-bit slide steps or as arpeggio offsets, and $05 $0C as the first two phase lengths.
One flag for each of the nine block swaps (block_swap), set while that swap is in effect: swaps_undo swaps back every one that is set.
Seven bytes after the swap flags that nothing reads.

The start-up the depacker jumps to, in what becomes the playfield's screen. Sets CIA 2's timer A to 2 cycles, turns all its interrupts off, starts the timer with the serial port as output, reads its interrupt register and writes the serial port's data register, so a byte is shifting out; copies cia2_serial_check's 21 bytes from $4030 to $0100; clears the depacker's jump address at $3DFE; and jumps to cold_start.
The 12 bytes of cia2_serial_check that the start-up copies to $0100; here they are only data.

Sprite shapes $10-$18, 64 bytes each (shape n at $4000 plus n times 64, in the video bank at $4000). $10-$13 the hero's legs walking left, under $14-$17, a soldier's top half walking left, which the hero and the white soldiers share (player_anim_tops, enemy_anim_tops; $14 is also the grenade thrower facing left); $18 the hero's top jumping left, over the legs $22.

Sprite shapes $19-$23: $19-$1C the hero's legs walking right under $1D-$20, the top walking right, shared with the white soldiers ($1D is also the grenade thrower facing right); $21 and $23 the hero's top and legs jumping right; $22 his legs jumping left.

Sprite shapes $24-$2F: $24-$27 the hero's two frames for a jump with no facing (tops $25, $27, legs $24, $26); $28 his legs on a ladder (with the top $A4); $29 his top stabbing left and $2B stabbing right, over walking legs; $2A the grenade thrower's top throwing left; $2C and $2D crouching right (legs, top) and $2E and $2F crouching left (top, legs). A crouching stab left is $2E over $C4, right $C3 over $2C.

Sprite shapes $30-$3F: $30-$33 a soldier's legs walking left and $34-$37 walking right, under the white and the blue soldiers' tops ($31 and $35 are also the officer's legs throwing); $38 and $39 the top and legs that type_top_shapes and type_bot_shapes give a white soldier (type 1) when he appears; $3A-$3D a soldier on a ladder (tops $3B and $3D, legs $3A and $3C); $3E a soldier's top jumping left; $3F the officer's top throwing.

Sprite shapes $40-$4F: $40 a soldier's top jumping right; $41 the officer's other throwing top (with $3F, one for each facing); $42-$45 legs walking left under $46-$49, the brown soldier's tops walking left; $4A-$4D legs walking right under $4E-$51, his tops walking right. The kicker and the bazooka man walk on the same legs.

Sprite shapes $50-$5F: $50 and $51 the last of the brown soldier's tops walking right; $52-$5D twelve shapes no shape table holds and no instruction loads, kneeling and leaping soldiers; $5E and $5F the crawler's legs and top, first frame.

Sprite shapes $60-$6F: $60 and $61 the crawler's second frame; $62-$64 an explosion's three frames (shot_explosion); $65 the bazooka shell facing left, also the jet's bomb, and $66 facing right; $67 a hand grenade, also the dropped weapon of types 0, 1 and 3; $68 a small ring no table selects; $69-$6B the flame thrower's three flames facing right; $6C and $6D the dropped bazooka and flame thrower (pickup_shapes); $6E the grenade thrower's legs facing left; $6F the lorry's front wheel, first frame.

Colours of tiles $10-$1F.

Colours of the ammunition icons on the status line, two bytes a weapon, read at the weapon times 2 less 2: 0 0 (unused), $09 brown for the bazooka, $0D light green for the grenades, $0F light grey for the flame thrower.
Writes the number of lives at $C408 on the status line, as a digit, or a space when there are none. The space comes from the LDA #$20 hidden in the BIT at $C267, which the branch for 0 lands on.
Writes the score's six decimal digits at $C433 on the status line, highest first, and a 0 after them: every score is ten times what the game counts.
Writes the hi score's six digits and a 0 after them at $C43D on the status line.
Adds the points waiting in points_due to the score, three bytes in decimal mode, and clears points_due.
Compares the score with the hi score from the highest byte down and, when it is higher, copies it over.
The score beats the hi score: copy its three bytes.
The intro's scene for picture_draw: the screen at $4000 cleared and filled with the four posts and the ground, in run-length commands ($FB run, $FC address, $FE colour, $FF end).
20 bytes nothing reads, after the end of picture_captives; from $C3F2 they decode as instructions that no path reaches.
The status band's screen, two rows at the top of the display: LIVES, SCORE, HI SCORE and STAGE on the first; on the second the ammunition icons at $C429, the score at $C433 and the hi score at $C43D.

Hands the virtual sprites to the multiplexer: copies their Y, X low and X high (21 each) into its own lists (mux_y, mux_xlo, mux_xhi), and the sorted order into mux_order too when the last sort changed it (order_changed). The multiplexer reads only these copies, so the main loop can move sprites while it runs.
The order is unchanged: copy only the positions.

The interrupt's first phase, which shares the 8 hardware sprites among the 21 virtual ones, run again and again down the playfield. Moves its raster threshold (mux_raster) 14 lines on and lets other interrupts in. Then, from mux_next back to the start of the order (sprites_sort leaves it in descending Y, so this goes from the top of the screen down), gives each sprite whose Y is under the threshold the next hardware sprite (mux_hw, 7 down to 0 and round again): its colour, its shape pointer (at $43F8 for the screen at $4000), its X and high bit and its Y. At the first sprite that is not yet due it sets the next raster interrupt 14 lines above it, or a few lines after the current one if that has passed, drops its return address and leaves the interrupt without moving on a phase, so that it runs again there.
The next virtual sprite in the order: place it, or wait for it.
7 bytes no path reaches: DEC mux_next, BMI, JMP $C47C, a copy of the end of the multiplexer's loop.
Every virtual sprite is placed: back to hardware sprite 7, mux_frames up by one, the next interrupt at raster $F6 (irq_status) and the threshold at $32. irq_start comes here too.
The next sprite is not due: the next interrupt goes 14 lines above it, or a few lines after the current one, and the interrupt ends at once (the two PLAs drop the return to irq).
The title page: draws the credits (text 0), shows the screen, starts the title tune ($35) and waits a frame at a time until fire is pressed, then blanks the screen again.

Draws text A (0-3) from text_table. The text's high address byte gets the stage's page offset (text_pages), as stages 2 and 3 keep their texts 6 pages higher. With the I/O switched out ($01 = $30) and interrupts off, it copies characters (AND $3F turns the letters into screen codes) to the address the STA at $C53B holds, moving along; a byte of $80 or more other than $FF is followed by a new address (low, high) to write to, and $FF ends the text.
STA $FFFF,X: its address (text_dest, the operand at $C53C) is set by each address in the text.
The operand of the STA at $C53B, where text_draw writes the next character; each address in a text sets it.
A marker byte: $FF ends the text; any other takes the next two bytes as the new address.
Page offsets text_draw adds to a text's address, by stage: 0, 0, 6, 6, and 0 for the ending.
Counts the frames the multiplexer finishes; nothing reads it.

Puts the virtual sprites back in their own order (sprite_order 0-20), zeroes all sixteen hardware sprite position registers, turns interrupts off and hands the sprites to the multiplexer (sprites_to_irq) and sorts them (sprites_sort); it returns with interrupts still off.
Three bytes after sprite_order_reset that nothing reads: $CE, $00, $00.

Ten sprite shapes for the Harbour's fight, which block swap 7 exchanges with shapes $C7-$D0: $C7 and $C8 the dog handler (handler_shapes), $C9-$CB and $CC-$CE the dogs running each way ($CA and $CD also their leap), $CF and $D0 a knifed dog, thrown into the air (dogs_hit).

The title's character set as loaded, which the status band shows in play and block swap 8 brings to $7800 for the title and the intermissions: $00 the copyright sign, $01-$1A the letters, $20 a space, $30-$39 the digits and $3A-$3E punctuation; $28-$2E and $40-$7F draw the intermission's scene.

Characters $80-$D0 of the title's set: the logo's pieces ($80-$91, $A0-$B0, $C0-$D0), more of the intermission's scene ($92-$98, $BB-$BF), the captives' posts ($99-$9F, $B1-$B5) and the ammunition icons $B6-$BA (ammo_icons). The swap ends at $CE87, where irq_start begins.

Points the interrupt vector at $FFFE to irq, lets only the VIC's raster interrupt in (CIA 1's timer interrupt is turned off and acknowledged), sets the phase to 0, the I/O in ($01 = $35), and goes to mux_done, which sets the first interrupt at raster $F6.

The raster interrupt. Saves the registers, acknowledges the VIC, clears decimal mode and calls the current phase (the JSR's operand at $CEB5): the multiplexer, irq_status or irq_playfield. Then moves irq_phase on, 0, 1, 2 and round, and puts the next phase's address from irq_phases into the JSR. The multiplexer can leave by irq_exit without coming back here, and then the phase stays.
The JSR to the current phase; its operand (irq_call, $CEB5) is rewritten after every phase.
The operand of the JSR at $CEB4, the current phase's address, rewritten by irq after every phase.
Restores X, Y and A and returns from the interrupt.

Sorts the 21 virtual sprites in descending order of Y, by insertion: sprite_order holds the sprite numbers, and each one with a higher Y than the one before it is moved back to its place. order_changed counts the moves, for sprites_to_irq. Then, with interrupts off, takes the scroll the main loop has used (scroll_step) from the scroll the interrupt has counted (scroll_pending).
The scroll bookkeeping: scroll_pending less scroll_step, or 0 when they are equal.

Draws picture A (0-3) from picture_table onto the screen at $4000, starting at its top left. Bytes below $FB are characters, written in the current colour (pic_colour) with the colour into colour RAM at the same place. Bytes $FB-$FF are commands, run through picture_commands by the JSR at $CF64.
A command: puts the handler's address from picture_commands into the JSR at $CF64 (its operand at $CF65) and calls it.
The JSR to the command's handler; its operand (pic_call) is written from picture_commands.
The operand of the JSR at $CF64.
Reads the picture's next byte and moves the pointer on.
Writes the character in A at the screen pointer, the colour pic_colour at the same place in colour RAM ($D800 plus the pointer's low 10 bits), and moves the pointer on.
The handlers of picture_draw's commands $FB-$FF: $CF9F run, $CFB3 address, $CFC8 skip, $CFBE colour, $CFC5 end.
Command $FB: a count and a character follow; writes the character that many times (a count of 0 writes it 256 times).
Command $FC: the next two bytes are the screen address to write at (low, high).
Command $FE: the next byte is the colour for the characters after it.
Command $FF: drops the return address of the command's JSR and returns from picture_draw itself.
Command $FD: skips 20 bytes of the picture. No picture uses it.
The character of the run being drawn.
The colour picture_draw writes into colour RAM.
Keeps the screen pointer's high byte while pic_put writes the colour.
The four pictures: 0 the intermission's map ($0434), 1 the intro's captives (picture_captives, $C300), 2 the title's logo ($03C0), 3 a blank screen ($06CE).

Puts every swapped block back: for each of the nine swaps, 8 down to 0, whose flag in swap_flags is set, swaps it again (block_swap). Keeps the interrupt flag as it was, as block_swap turns interrupts on.

The ammunition icons on the status line, two characters each, read at the weapon times 2 less 2: $B6 $B7 (unused), $B6 $B7 the bazooka, $BA and a space a grenade, $B8 $B9 the flame thrower, then $C2 $60 that nothing reads.
A byte nothing reads.

Under the I/O area: the Harbour's characters $40-$C7, which block swap 0 exchanges with $7A00 for the Harbour, its sea, ships, warehouses and cranes. Once swapped this holds the texts, which is why text_draw reads them 6 pages higher on stages 2 and 3.
The rest of the Harbour's characters past the first 1024 bytes: $C0-$C7, the last 64 bytes block swap 0 moves (to $7E00-$7E3F).

Under the I/O area: the Prison Camp's characters $60-$B9, which block swap 4 exchanges with $7B00 after the Bridge's set is in, for the camp's walls and buildings. $D640 holds its mine, $A0 and $A1, whose original anim_chars_restore puts back.
240 bytes nothing reads: characters laid out like $E2-$FF of the Bridge's set at $DF10, and the same but for three of them ($EE, $EF and $F8).

Under the I/O area and colour RAM: the first half of the Bridge's character set, characters $00-$7F; the rest, $80-$FF, is at $DC00 (chars_bridge_b). Block swap 3 exchanges all 2 KB, $D800-$DFFF, with $7800. The code that scrolls colour RAM reads and writes these addresses with the I/O switched in, so it never sees this RAM. $DA90 holds the Bridge's mine, $52 and $53.
The Bridge's characters $80-$FF, under the I/O area ($DC00-$DFFF: the two CIAs and the I/O 1 and 2 areas), and from $C8 its ladders and floors.
Starts the sound effect at A (low), Y (high) on voice 1: sfx_start with X = 0.

Starts the 31-byte sound effect at A (low), Y (high) on voice X (0-2 for SID voices 1-3). The music may no longer write the voice (its free flag, v1_free plus X, cleared) and its control register is set to $02, the gate off. Bytes $16-$1A go to the voice's pulse width, waveform, attack/decay and sustain/release registers, through the STA at $E01E whose operand ($E01F) is set to the voice's register offset from sfx_reg_offsets; bytes $1D-$1E are the frequency. Then the voice's live effect (its block, ending at the offset in sfx_block_ends) takes bytes 0-$17, the frequency effect and pulse sweep settings with the start width, and the waveform byte, gate time, sound time and frequency. Last it starts the pulse sweep and the frequency slide that the bytes ask for.

STA $D400+r,X for the effect's register bytes, X 4 down to 0, where r, the operand's low byte (sfx_reg), is the voice's pulse width register ($02, $09 or $10, from sfx_reg_offsets); the snapshot holds $09.
The operand's low byte of the STA at $E01E, set by sfx_start to the voice's register offset.
After the copy X is the voice's block offset less 23: 0 for voice 1, $27 for voice 2, $4E for voice 3.
Voice 1: starts the pulse sweep if the effect has one, then the frequency slide; the slide is left alone only when there is a sweep and no frequency effect.
Starts voice 1's frequency slide from the note's frequency (v1_note_freq into v1_freq) and falls into v1_slide_again.
Reloads the four phase counters of voice 1's slide (v1_slide_counts) from its phase lengths (v1_slide_times), so the four phases run again from the frequency it has reached.
Voice 2 or 3: voice 3 is the block offset $4E.
Voice 2: start the pulse sweep if the effect has one, then the frequency slide if it has one.
Starts voice 2's frequency slide from the note's frequency (v2_note_freq into v2_freq) and falls into v2_slide_again.
Reloads the four phase counters of voice 2's slide from its phase lengths.
Voice 3: start the pulse sweep if the effect has one, then the frequency slide if it has one.
Starts voice 3's frequency slide from the note's frequency (v3_note_freq into v3_freq) and falls into v3_slide_again.
Reloads the four phase counters of voice 3's slide from its phase lengths.

Voice 1's note reader, run once a frame by frame_wait. While its tune plays (v1_playing) it counts down the note's duration (v1_duration); when that runs out it reads the pattern's next events, commands first, up to the next note or rest.
Moves the pattern pointer (v1_pattern) on by 3 bytes, the length of most commands, or from $E10E by the count in A, and reads the next event.
Reads the next byte of voice 1's pattern. $C0 or more is a command: its handler's address comes from v1_commands and is written into the JMP at $E12C, which goes there. Below $C0 it is a note.

Voice 1's JMP to the command's handler: its operand is rewritten for each command. Each handler goes on to the next event itself, except a return ($C0) with nothing to return to, which ends the voice (v1_playing) and returns.
The operand of voice 1's JMP at $E12C, the handler of the command being read, from v1_commands.
Voice 1: a rest, or a note while a sound effect has the voice; only the duration is read.

A note: bytes $00-$5E are notes, $60-$BE the same notes with their duration given in frames; $5F and $BF are rests. The note plus the transpose (v1_transpose) indexes note_freq_lo and note_freq_hi. Unless a sound effect has the voice (v1_free is 0) it plays it: the test bit restarts the oscillator, then the instrument's sustain/release, attack/decay and waveform byte (with its bit 3 cleared, the gate in bit 0), the pulse width (v1_pulse_width) and the frequency, kept in v1_note_freq.
Voice 1: with a pulse sweep set (v1_pulse_fx_set) its settings are copied into the live ones: the start width, the two steps, the delay and the two phase lengths.

Voice 1's copy stores the start width's low byte back where it read it ($EC1E) rather than in v1_pulse_start, as voices 2 and 3 do at $E53D and $E8E9: a sweep that starts again (v1_pulse_restart) takes its low byte from whatever was last left there.

Voice 1: with a frequency effect set (v1_freq_fx_set) its 13 settings are copied into the live ones (v1_slide_steps on), and the effect starts: an arpeggio (bit 3) takes the note as its base, a slide starts from the note's frequency (v1_slide_start).
Voice 1: the instrument's gate time and sound time go live (v1_gate_time, v1_sound_time).

Reads the duration after a note or rest: for a note byte below $60 it is an index into durations (3 frames a step), for one of $60 or more a number of frames. Puts it in v1_duration and moves the pointer past the two bytes.

Voice 1's command $C0, the end of a pattern: returns to the place the last call saved on voice 1's stack (v1_stack_lo, v1_stack_hi). At the outermost level, the stack index back at 8, the voice's tune ends (v1_playing cleared).
Voice 1's command $CC, count: starts a repeat. Saves the place after the command and the count on the stack (v1_stack_count) and goes on.
Voice 1's command $CE: counts the innermost repeat down. Until it reaches 0 the pattern goes back to the place the repeat saved; then the repeat is dropped from the stack and the pattern goes on.
Voice 1's command $D6, address: copies the five-byte instrument at the address into v1_instrument: waveform, attack/decay, sustain/release, gate time and sound time.
Voice 1's command $D4, address: copies 14 bytes from the address into the frequency effect's settings (v1_fx, $EC08-$EC15), its flags included.
Voice 1's command $D2, address: copies 10 bytes from the address into the frequency effect's settings: the four steps and the first two phase lengths.

Voice 1's command $D0, last index, last offset, address: copies bytes from the address into the settings (v1_fx onwards), ending at v1_fx plus the index and taking the offset plus one bytes. Moves on 5 bytes.
Voice 1's command $C8, transpose, address: sets the transpose and goes on at the address.
Voice 1's command $C4, address: goes on at the address.
Voice 1's command $C6, transpose, address: sets the transpose and calls the pattern at the address, saving the place after the command on the stack for the $C0 that ends it.
Voice 1's calls: saves the return place (the pointer plus A) on the stack and jumps to the address at offset X of the command.
Voice 1's command $C2, address: calls the pattern at the address, saving the place after the command on the stack.
Voice 1's command $DA, transpose: sets the number of semitones added to every note after it.
Voice 1's command $CA, index, value: sets one byte of the settings, v1_fx plus the index, for the notes after it.
Voice 1's command $D8, index, value: sets one byte of the live effect, v1_slide_steps plus the index, which changes the note already sounding.

Voice 1's effects, run every frame by irq_player. Nothing while its sound time (v1_sound_time) is 0. First the gate: with bit 3 of the waveform byte (v1_control) the gate goes off when the note has fewer frames left than v1_gate_time, otherwise after v1_gate_time frames; then v1_sound_time counts down and at 0 the voice's seven SID registers are cleared and the voice is free for the music again (v1_free). Then the pulse sweep and the frequency effect.
Voice 1: the gate time counts down to the gate going off; then the sound time counts down to silence.

Voice 1's pulse sweep, when one is on (v1_pulse_fx): after its delay (v1_pulse_delay) the width (v1_pulse) moves by the first step for v1_pulse_counts frames and by the second for the next count. At the end, flag bit 7 starts it again from the start width (v1_pulse_restart) and bit 0 runs the two phases again from where it is (v1_pulse_again); with neither it stays. Writes the width to the SID.

Voice 1's frequency effect, when one is on (v1_freq_fx). Bit 3 is an arpeggio; otherwise a slide in four phases after a delay (v1_slide_delay); with bit 1 the fourth phase's step is applied during the delay too.

Voice 1's arpeggio: each frame the next offset from v1_slide_steps, counting down from the length in v1_slide_times+3 and round again, is added to the base note (v1_slide_times+2) and that note's frequency is written to the SID.
Voice 1's slide: the frequency (v1_freq) moves by each of the four steps (v1_slide_steps) for its phase's count of frames (v1_slide_counts), in turn, and is written to the SID.

Voice 1, all four phases of the slide done: flag bit 7 starts the slide again from the note's frequency (v1_slide_start) and bit 0 runs the phases again from where it is (v1_slide_again), a vibrato; with neither the frequency stays.

Voice 2's note reader, run once a frame by frame_wait. While its tune plays (v2_playing) it counts down the note's duration (v2_duration); when that runs out it reads the pattern's next events, commands first, up to the next note or rest.
Moves the pattern pointer (v2_pattern) on by 3 bytes, the length of most commands, or from $E4BB by the count in A, and reads the next event.
Reads the next byte of voice 2's pattern. $C0 or more is a command: its handler's address comes from v2_commands and is written into the JMP at $E4D9, which goes there. Below $C0 it is a note.

Voice 2's JMP to the command's handler: its operand is rewritten for each command. Each handler goes on to the next event itself, except a return ($C0) with nothing to return to, which ends the voice (v2_playing) and returns.
The operand of voice 2's JMP at $E4D9, the handler of the command being read, from v2_commands.
Voice 2: a rest, or a note while a sound effect has the voice; only the duration is read.

When the score reaches next_life: moves next_life on by 70,000 (its middle byte plus $70, in decimal), and gives an extra life if the hero has fewer than 9, redrawing the lives. The first is at 30,000, set by new_game, so they come at 30,000, 100,000, 170,000 and so on; at 9 lives the extra life is lost.

Swaps block A (0-8) with its partner, byte for byte, and flips its flag in swap_flags. The memory configuration comes from swap_ports and is written into the LDA at $FF21: $30, all RAM, for a block under the I/O, with interrupts off while the I/O is gone; $35 for the others. Whole pages first, then the remaining bytes (its count in the CPY at $FF55). Ends with the I/O in and interrupts on.
The operand of LDA at $FF21: the swap's memory configuration, from swap_ports.
The bytes after the whole pages.
The operand of CPY at $FF55: how many bytes after the whole pages, from the low byte of swap_lengths.
The block each is swapped with: $7A00, $A000, $B000, $7800, $7B00, $A200, $B200, $71C0, $7800.
The memory configuration for each swap: $30 (all RAM) for swaps 0, 3 and 4, whose first block is under the I/O, $35 for the others.

Draws the weapon's ammunition on the status line from $C429: an icon two characters wide for each round left (ammo_icons, coloured from ammo_colours), up to five, with spaces after them. With no weapon it draws nothing; with one round left it leaves the icon already there.
Blank the places after the last round, from the fifth down.
Draw an icon for each round, from the last down to the first.
21 bytes of $AA filler that nothing reads.
The NMI vector, $FFFC: the RESTORE key's interrupt goes to the RTI there and does nothing.
The RTI ($40) the NMI vector points at. With the vector beside it, the two bytes also read as the reset vector, $4040, which a real reset never uses, as the ROM is switched in then.
The interrupt vector, set to irq ($CEA9) by irq_start.
